specStatements.text: Substances may move into and out of cells across the cell membranes via diffusion.

Diffusion is the spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

Some of the substances transported in and out of cells by diffusion are oxygen and carbon dioxide in gas exchange, and of the waste product urea from cells into the blood plasma for excretion in the kidney.
Students should be able to explain how different factors affect the rate of diffusion.
Factors which affect the rate of diffusion are: the difference in concentrations (concentration gradient); the temperature; the surface area of the membrane.
A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio. This allows sufficient transport of molecules into and out of the cell to meet the needs of the organism.
Students should be able to calculate and compare surface area to volume ratios.
Students should be able to explain the need for exchange surfaces and a transport system in multicellular organisms in terms of surface area to volume ratio.
Students should be able to explain how the small intestine and lungs in mammals, gills in fish, and the roots and leaves in plants, are adapted for exchanging materials.

In multicellular organisms, surfaces and organ systems are specialised for exchanging materials. This is to allow sufficient molecules to be transported into and out of cells for the organism's needs. The effectiveness of an exchange surface is increased by: having a large surface area; a membrane that is thin, to provide a short diffusion path; (in animals) having an efficient blood supply; (in animals, for gaseous exchange) being ventilated.
Water may move across cell membranes via osmosis. Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
Students should be able to: use simple compound measures of rate of water uptake; use percentiles; calculate percentage gain and loss of mass of plant tissue.
Students should be able to plot, draw and interpret appropriate graphs.
Active transport moves substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution (against a concentration gradient). This requires energy from respiration.
Active transport allows mineral ions to be absorbed into plant root hairs from very dilute solutions in the soil. Plants require ions for healthy growth.
It also allows sugar molecules to be absorbed from lower concentrations in the gut into the blood which has a higher sugar concentration. Sugar molecules are used for cell respiration.
Students should be able to: describe how substances are transported into and out of cells by diffusion, osmosis and active transport; explain the differences between the three processes.

concepts.definition: The spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. Substances may move into and out of cells across the cell membranes via diffusion, and no energy from respiration is needed.

The difference in concentrations of a substance between two areas. Diffusion gives a net movement down a concentration gradient, from the area of higher concentration to the area of lower concentration; the greater the difference in concentrations, the faster the rate of diffusion.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the rate of diffusion
concepts.definition: The factors which affect the rate of diffusion are the difference in concentrations (concentration gradient), the temperature, and the surface area of the membrane. Increasing any one of these increases the rate of diffusion.

Substances transported in and out of cells by diffusion include oxygen and carbon dioxide in gas exchange, and the waste product urea, which moves from cells into the blood plasma for excretion in the kidney.

The surface area of an organism or cell compared with its volume. A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio, which allows sufficient transport of molecules into and out of the cell to meet the needs of the organism. The ratio gets smaller as an organism gets larger.

A surface in a multicellular organism that is specialised for exchanging materials, so that sufficient molecules can be transported into and out of cells for the organism's needs. Its effectiveness is increased by having a large surface area, a membrane that is thin, (in animals) an efficient blood supply and, in animals for gaseous exchange, being ventilated.
The short distance a substance has to travel across an exchange surface. A membrane that is thin provides a short diffusion path, which increases the effectiveness of the exchange surface.

The small intestine and lungs in mammals, gills in fish, and the roots and leaves in plants are adapted for exchange by having a large surface area and a thin membrane that gives a short diffusion path. The small intestine, lungs and gills also have an efficient blood supply, and the lungs are ventilated.
The diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. Water may move across cell membranes via osmosis.
A membrane that allows water molecules through but not all of the dissolved solute particles. Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane.
The movement of substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution, that is against a concentration gradient. This requires energy from respiration.

concepts.term: Mineral ion uptake by root hairs
concepts.definition: Active transport allows mineral ions to be absorbed into plant root hairs from very dilute solutions in the soil, against a concentration gradient. Plants require ions for healthy growth.
Active transport allows sugar molecules to be absorbed from lower concentrations in the gut into the blood, which has a higher sugar concentration. Sugar molecules are used for cell respiration.

misconceptions.question: Does diffusion need energy from respiration?
misconceptions.correct: No. Diffusion is a net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration and needs no energy from respiration.
misconceptions.misconception: Diffusion, like active transport, uses energy from respiration to move particles across the cell membrane.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three transport processes are taught together, and students treat any movement of particles as something that has to be powered, so they attach the energy requirement of active transport to diffusion as well.
misconceptions.correction: Diffusion is the spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. Only active transport, which moves substances against a concentration gradient, requires energy from respiration.

misconceptions.question: In osmosis, which way does water move through a partially permeable membrane?
misconceptions.correct: Water moves from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Water moves from the concentrated solution to the dilute solution, because water flows away from the side that has most dissolved solute.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly remember that diffusion goes from higher to lower concentration, but apply it to the solute they can see rather than to the water molecules that actually cross the membrane.
misconceptions.correction: Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. The dilute solution is the one with the higher concentration of water.

misconceptions.question: What moves through the partially permeable membrane during osmosis?
misconceptions.misconception: Dissolved solutes such as sugar cross the membrane along with the water during osmosis.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Osmosis is introduced as a type of diffusion, so students assume any dissolved particle can cross, and diagrams showing solute particles on both sides of the membrane reinforce the idea.
misconceptions.correction: Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. It is the water that moves across the membrane.

misconceptions.question: How does the surface area to volume ratio change as an organism gets bigger?
misconceptions.misconception: A bigger organism has a bigger surface area to volume ratio, because it has a bigger surface area.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare surface areas instead of ratios. Because a large organism obviously has more surface, they conclude that the ratio must be larger too.
misconceptions.correction: Volume increases faster than surface area, so the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases. A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio, which allows sufficient transport of molecules into and out of the cell to meet the needs of the organism.

misconceptions.question: Which process moves substances against a concentration gradient?
misconceptions.misconception: Diffusion and active transport move substances in the same direction, so diffusion can move substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both processes are described as getting substances into cells, so students focus on the destination rather than on the concentrations on each side of the membrane.
misconceptions.correction: Diffusion results in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. Active transport moves substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution, against a concentration gradient, and this requires energy from respiration.

misconceptions.question: How does a bigger difference in concentrations affect the rate of diffusion?
misconceptions.correct: It increases the rate of diffusion.
misconceptions.misconception: A big difference in concentrations slows diffusion down, because crowded particles collide and get in each other's way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture a crowd of particles as blocked rather than as more likely to spread outwards, and everyday experience of crowds slowing movement supports the idea.
misconceptions.correction: The difference in concentrations (concentration gradient) is one of the factors which affect the rate of diffusion: the greater the difference in concentrations, the faster the rate of diffusion.

misconceptions.question: Which factors affect the rate of diffusion?
misconceptions.correct: The difference in concentrations, the temperature and the surface area of the membrane.
misconceptions.misconception: Temperature is what sets the rate of diffusion, so if the temperature stays the same the rate cannot change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Particle theory is usually taught through heating and cooling, so students tie particle movement to temperature alone and overlook the other factors.
misconceptions.correction: Factors which affect the rate of diffusion are: the difference in concentrations (concentration gradient); the temperature; the surface area of the membrane. Changing any one of these changes the rate of diffusion.

misconceptions.question: How is the percentage gain or loss of mass of plant tissue calculated?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the change in mass by the starting mass, then multiply by 100.
misconceptions.misconception: The percentage change in mass is worked out from the final mass, either by dividing the change by the final mass or by comparing the final and starting masses directly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students use the mass they measured last as the reference value, and percentages are often first met as a part of a total rather than as a change from a starting value.
misconceptions.correction: Percentage gain or loss of mass of plant tissue = (change in mass divided by the starting mass) multiplied by 100. The starting mass is the value that the change is divided by.

misconceptions.question: How are mineral ions absorbed into plant root hairs from the soil?
misconceptions.correct: By active transport, which requires energy from respiration.
misconceptions.misconception: Mineral ions enter root hair cells, and sugar enters the blood from the gut, by diffusion down a concentration gradient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diffusion is met first and is the process students reach for by default, so they assume a substance entering a cell must be more concentrated outside without checking the actual concentrations.
misconceptions.correction: Active transport allows mineral ions to be absorbed into plant root hairs from very dilute solutions in the soil, and sugar molecules to be absorbed from lower concentrations in the gut into the blood which has a higher sugar concentration. Both are movements against a concentration gradient and require energy from respiration.

misconceptions.question: What makes an exchange surface effective?
misconceptions.correct: A large surface area and a membrane that is thin.
misconceptions.misconception: An exchange surface works better if it is thick and small, because that holds substances in place long enough for them to be taken up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of absorption as soaking up and storing, so a thick, compact surface seems better than one that is thin and spread out.
misconceptions.correction: The effectiveness of an exchange surface is increased by: having a large surface area; a membrane that is thin, to provide a short diffusion path; (in animals) having an efficient blood supply; (in animals, for gaseous exchange) being ventilated.

mcqs.stem: In diffusion, the particles of a substance in solution show a net movement:

options.text: from a lower to a higher concentration, requiring energy from respiration
options.rationale: A student who believes diffusion and active transport move substances in the same direction picks the option that describes active transport in full. It is wrong because diffusion gives a net movement from higher to lower concentration; only active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient.

options.text: from a lower to a higher concentration, using no energy
options.rationale: A student holding the belief that diffusion can move substances up a concentration gradient chooses this because it keeps diffusion passive but reverses the direction. It is wrong because the net movement in diffusion is from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

options.text: from a higher to a lower concentration, without energy
options.rationale: Diffusion is the spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, and it does not require energy from respiration.

options.text: from a higher to a lower concentration, requiring energy
options.rationale: A student who believes diffusion uses energy from respiration gets the direction right but adds an energy requirement. It is wrong because only active transport requires energy from respiration; diffusion is a net movement down a concentration gradient with no energy needed.

mcqs.stem: The concentration of oxygen in the air inside the alveoli is raised. Everything else, including the temperature, stays the same. What happens to the rate of diffusion of oxygen into the blood?

options.text: It falls, as a steeper gradient crowds particles
options.rationale: A student who believes a big difference in concentrations blocks particle movement reads a steeper gradient as crowding. It is wrong because the greater the difference in concentrations, the faster the rate of diffusion.

options.text: It stays the same, as the temperature has not risen
options.rationale: A student who believes temperature alone sets the rate of diffusion concludes that an unchanged temperature means an unchanged rate. It is wrong because the difference in concentrations is also a factor which affects the rate of diffusion.

options.text: It falls, because the particles collide with one another
options.rationale: The same belief that crowded particles get in each other's way leads a student to expect collisions to slow diffusion down. It is wrong because a greater difference in concentrations increases the rate of diffusion.

options.text: It rises, as the concentration gradient is steeper
options.rationale: The difference in concentrations (concentration gradient) is a factor which affects the rate of diffusion, so raising the oxygen concentration in the alveoli increases the rate at which oxygen diffuses into the blood.

mcqs.stem: Cube A has sides 1 mm long. Cube B has sides 2 mm long. Which statement about their surface area to volume ratios is correct?

options.text: Cube A has a ratio of 3:1 and cube B one of 6:1
options.rationale: A student who believes a bigger object has a bigger surface area to volume ratio gives the larger ratio to cube B. It is wrong because cube A has a surface area of 6 mm2 and a volume of 1 mm3, giving 6:1, while cube B has 24 mm2 and 8 mm3, giving 3:1.

options.text: Cube A has a ratio of 6:1 and cube B a ratio of 3:1
options.rationale: Cube A: surface area 6 mm2, volume 1 mm3, ratio 6:1. Cube B: surface area 24 mm2, volume 8 mm3, ratio 3:1. The smaller cube has the relatively large surface area to volume ratio, as a single-celled organism does.

options.text: Cube A has a ratio of 3:1 and cube B one of 12:1
options.rationale: The same belief makes the ratio rise steeply with size, so the student assigns the largest value to the largest cube. It is wrong because volume increases faster than surface area, so the ratio falls from 6:1 to 3:1.

options.text: Cube A has a ratio of 6:1 and cube B a ratio of 12:1
options.rationale: A student who works out cube A correctly but still believes the ratio grows with size doubles it for cube B. It is wrong because cube B's surface area is 24 mm2 and its volume is 8 mm3, giving a ratio of 3:1.

mcqs.stem: Why do large multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces and a transport system?

options.text: Their surface area to volume ratio is too small for diffusion
options.rationale: A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio, which allows sufficient transport of molecules to meet its needs. In a large multicellular organism the ratio is too small for diffusion across the outer surface to supply enough molecules, so surfaces and organ systems are specialised for exchanging materials and a transport system carries them to the cells.

options.text: Their surface area to volume ratio is too high for diffusion
options.rationale: A student who believes a large organism has a large surface area to volume ratio still remembers that a transport system is needed, so pairs the two. It is wrong because a large ratio would allow enough diffusion; it is the small ratio that creates the problem.

options.text: Their surface area to volume ratio increases as they get bigger
options.rationale: This states the belief directly: that growth raises the ratio because surface area grows. It is wrong because volume increases faster than surface area, so the ratio decreases as the organism gets bigger.

options.text: Their surface area to volume ratio grows with their surface area
options.rationale: A student comparing surface areas rather than ratios treats more surface as automatically meaning a higher ratio. It is wrong because the ratio depends on surface area compared with volume, and volume rises faster.

mcqs.stem: Which feature of the alveoli in the lungs increases the effectiveness of gas exchange?

options.text: A thick wall holding the gases in for longer
options.rationale: A student who believes a thick exchange surface holds substances while they are taken up chooses the thicker wall. It is wrong because a thick membrane gives a long diffusion path, which slows the rate of diffusion.

options.text: A small surface area that packs cells in
options.rationale: The same belief treats a compact surface as more efficient. It is wrong because the effectiveness of an exchange surface is increased by having a large surface area, which is why the lungs contain many alveoli.

options.text: A thin wall that provides a short diffusion path
options.rationale: The effectiveness of an exchange surface is increased by a membrane that is thin, to provide a short diffusion path, so oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse quickly between the alveoli and the blood.

options.text: A thick wall that slows the escape of gases
options.rationale: A student thinking of exchange as trapping substances sees a thick wall as useful. It is wrong because the point of the alveolar wall is to allow rapid diffusion, which needs a thin membrane and a short diffusion path.

mcqs.stem: Osmosis takes place through a partially permeable membrane. Which statement describes it correctly?

options.text: Water moves from a concentrated solution to a dilute one
options.rationale: A student who believes water flows away from the side with most solute reverses the direction. It is wrong because osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution.

options.text: Water moves from a dilute to a concentrated solution
options.rationale: Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.

options.text: Sugar moves from a dilute solution into a concentrated one
options.rationale: A student who believes solutes cross the membrane during osmosis substitutes sugar for water. It is wrong because it is water that diffuses through the partially permeable membrane in osmosis.

options.text: Solutes move from a concentrated solution to a dilute one
options.rationale: The same belief about solutes crossing the membrane, combined with ordinary diffusion of the solute, produces this answer. It is wrong because osmosis is defined as the diffusion of water, not of the dissolved solutes.

mcqs.stem: A potato cylinder has a mass of 4.0 g at the start. After 30 minutes in a sugar solution its mass is 3.4 g. What is the percentage loss of mass, and how is it found?

options.text: 17.6%, dividing the change by the final mass
options.rationale: A student who uses the last mass measured as the reference divides 0.6 g by 3.4 g. It is wrong because percentage gain or loss of mass is found from the starting mass, not the final mass.

options.text: 15.0%, dividing the change by the starting mass
options.rationale: The change in mass is 4.0 g minus 3.4 g, which is 0.6 g. Percentage loss of mass = (0.6 divided by 4.0) multiplied by 100 = 15.0%, using the starting mass of the plant tissue.

options.text: 85.0%, dividing the final mass by the start mass
options.rationale: A student who compares the final and starting masses directly, without first finding the change, gets the mass remaining rather than the change. It is wrong because percentage change uses the change in mass, not the final mass, as the numerator.

options.text: 117.6%, dividing start mass by the final mass
options.rationale: The same failure to work with the change in mass, with the two masses the other way round, gives a value above 100%. It is wrong because percentage loss of mass = (change in mass divided by starting mass) multiplied by 100.

mcqs.stem: A student plots percentage change in mass of potato cylinders on the y-axis against concentration of sugar solution on the x-axis. The line crosses the x-axis, at zero percentage change in mass, at 0.30 mol/dm3. What does this point show?

options.text: Water moved into the cells from the sugar solution
options.rationale: A student who believes water moves from the concentrated solution into the cells expects water to enter here. It is wrong because there is no change in mass, so there has been no net movement of water by osmosis.

options.text: The sugar moved out of the cells into the sugar solution
options.rationale: A student who believes dissolved solutes cross the partially permeable membrane during osmosis explains the zero reading as sugar leaving the cells. It is wrong because osmosis is the diffusion of water, not of the dissolved sugar, and a zero change in mass shows no net movement of water.

options.text: The sugar moved from the solution into the cells
options.rationale: A student who believes solutes cross the partially permeable membrane explains the zero reading by sugar entering. It is wrong because osmosis is the diffusion of water through the membrane, and a zero change in mass shows no net water movement.

options.text: The cells and the solution had equal concentrations
options.rationale: At zero percentage change in mass there is no net movement of water by osmosis, so the cell contents and the external solution are at the same concentration, and 0.30 mol/dm3 is the concentration inside the potato cells.

mcqs.stem: Root hair cells take up mineral ions from a very dilute solution in the soil. How are the mineral ions taken up?

options.text: By active transport, which uses energy from respiration
options.rationale: Active transport moves substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution, against a concentration gradient, and requires energy from respiration. This allows mineral ions to be absorbed into plant root hairs from very dilute solutions in the soil.

options.text: By diffusion, moving down the concentration gradient
options.rationale: A student who assumes any substance entering a cell must be more concentrated outside chooses diffusion. It is wrong because the solution in the soil is very dilute, so the ions move against a concentration gradient.

options.text: By osmosis, across the partially permeable membrane
options.rationale: A student who believes dissolved solutes cross the membrane during osmosis applies osmosis to the mineral ions. It is wrong because osmosis is the diffusion of water, not of mineral ions.

options.text: By diffusion, moving up the concentration gradient
options.rationale: A student who believes diffusion and active transport move substances the same way gets the direction right but names the wrong process. It is wrong because movement from a more dilute to a more concentrated solution is active transport and requires energy from respiration.
